extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and natural philosophers (19th-century audience interested in astronomy and geognosy)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for conducting and interpreting astronomical and terrestrial (geognostic) observations in natural philosophy: how to gather, quantify, and reason from telescopic/star-gauging, parallax and orbital measurements, stratigraphic evidence, and limits of direct access to Earth's interior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical grounding of physical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of physical laws is revealed to us by many phenomena (for instance, by the motion of double stars, and by the amount of retarded or accelerated motion in different parts of their elliptic orbits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer basing assertions about universal forces on multiple independent phenomena rather than vague conjecture or undefined analogies. Use observed deviations and patterns in celestial motions as primary evidence for laws of attraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on improved observations and calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Human inquiry need no longer pursue this subject in the domain of vague conjecture, for the progress made in the method of astronomical observations and calculations has enabled astronomy to take up its position on a firm basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize methodological improvements: systematic observation, precise positional measures, and rigorous calculation are the basis for reliable astronomical knowledge. Upgrade claims as measurement precision improves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deriving orbital elements and masses from positional and temporal measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: By a skillful combination of the altered distances and angles of position, the elements of these orbits may be found, conclusions drawn regarding the absolute distance of the double stars from the Earth, and comparisons made between their mass and that of the Sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use changes in distance and position angle over time (periods of revolution, altered distances, angles) to compute orbital elements, deduce absolute distances, and estimate component masses. Provide worked combinations of positional and temporal data when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of parallax measurements to determine distances and infer masses
rubrics_metrics.description: The distance of the star 61 Cygni, made known by Bessel, has led approximately to a knowledge of the quantity of matter contained in this body as a double star.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallax determinations (even when small) are fundamental to converting angular/photometric measures into physical distances and then into mass estimations for binaries. Treat parallax results as enabling quantitative, not merely qualitative, inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit acknowledgement of measurement uncertainties
rubrics_metrics.description: The comparison of the volume of the Sun with that of the fixed stars of the first magnitude is dependent upon the apparent diameter of the latter bodies -- an extremely undertain optical element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state uncertainties and sensitivity to poorly-known optical elements (e.g., apparent diameters). Avoid overconfident conclusions when core inputs are 'extremely uncertain'; present ranges or conditional statements tied to assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautious use of analogy and inductive generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The analogies deduced from the relatively larger mass of those planets in our solar system that are attended by satellites ... have led other astronomers to conjecture that the average mass of the larger number of the binary stars exceeds the mass of the Sun. We are, however, far from having arrived at general results regarding this subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogical reasoning (e.g., comparing planet–satellite relations to binary-star systems) is useful but must be flagged as conjectural until supported by direct measurement; avoid treating analogies as definitive proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical star-gauging to infer galactic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The two brilliant nodes in which the branches of the zone unite ... appear to exercise a powerful attraction on the contiguous stars; in the most brilliant part ... one half of the 330,000 stars that have been discovered in a breadth of 5 degrees are directed toward one side, and the remainder to the other. It is in this part that Herschel supposes the layer to be broken up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use counts, directional distributions, and spatial statistics of star positions (star-gauging) to infer large-scale structures (rings, breaks, nodes) of the Milky Way or stellar strata. Report sampling breadth and any anisotropies observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative scaling and contextual comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of telescopic stars in the Milky Way uninterrupted by any nebulae is estimated at 18 millions. ... there are not in the whole heavens more than about 8000 stars between the first and the sixth magnitudes, visible to the naked eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When giving large numerical estimates, provide comparative reference points (e.g., naked-eye stars vs telescopic counts) to convey scale and significance. Use such comparisons to make large numbers comprehensible and relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for perceptual and instrumental biases in photometry
rubrics_metrics.description: As the retina retains a less vivid impression of separate than of infinitely near luminous points, less strongly marked photometric relations are excited in the latter case, as Arago has recently shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct for human-perception effects and instrument response when interpreting brightness and photometric relations; be wary of raw visual impressions and provide calibration or instrumental photometry where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor observation over speculative assumptions about cosmic distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: The assumption of such a distribution in space [an infinite uniform filling of stars] is, however, at variance with observation, which shows us large starless regions of space, 'openings' in the heavens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let empirical observations (e.g., starless regions, clusters) challenge and refine theoretical assumptions; do not cling to elegant but unobserved models when data indicate otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret astronomical observations as access to the past (finite light speed)
rubrics_metrics.description: These events in the universe belong, however, with reference to their historical reality, to other periods of time than those in which the phenomena of light are first revealed to the inhabitants of the Earth ... with our large and powerful telescopic instruments we penetrate alike through the boundaries of time and space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always account for light-travel time when interpreting the state of remote objects: observed radiation is evidence of a past state. Phrase conclusions in temporal terms and avoid assuming contemporaneity of distant phenomena with present Earth time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline of geognostic parameters to be investigated
rubrics_metrics.description: It will be expedient to cast a preliminary glance over the relations in space of solids and fluids, the form of the Earth, its mean density, and the partial distribution of this density in the interior of our planet, its temperature and its electro-magnetic tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comprehensive geognostic investigation should include: solid/fluid spatial relations, Earth shape, mean and partial density distribution, internal temperature profiles, and electromagnetic conditions. Use this checklist to structure terrestrial studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use surface geology, stratigraphy and fossils to infer interior history
rubrics_metrics.description: The study of the strata which are so differently formed and arranged before our eyes, and of all that has been so variously dislocated, conforted, and upheaved, by mutual compression and volcanic force, leads the reflective observer, by simple analogies, to draw a comparison between the present and an age that has long passed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ stratigraphic relations, deformation patterns, fossil content, and sedimentary structures to reconstruct past environments and infer internal geological processes. Combine observation with analogy and scaling to extend inference beyond directly exposed strata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of direct human access and use natural probes
rubrics_metrics.description: These labors do not extend beyond a vertical depth of somewhat more than 2000 feet ... The crystalline masses that have been erupted from active volcanoes ... have come from depths which ... must certainly be sixty times greater than those to which human labor has been enabled to penetrate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify the limits of direct study (deepest mines, borings) and complement them by studying natural processes (volcanic ejecta, hot springs) that sample deeper layers. Treat volcanic products as natural 'cores' from depths unreachable by human excavation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use barometric and dip measurements to infer depths and basin geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: We are able to give in numbers the depth of the shaft where the strata of coal, after penetrating a certain way, rise again at a distance that admits of being accurately defined by measurements. These dips show that the carboniferous strata ... must lie ... more than five or six thousand feet below the present level of the sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply barometric and hypsometric measurements and measured dips of strata to calculate subsurface basin depths and stratigraphic extent. Present numerical estimates with the assumptions and methods used (e.g., barometric conversions, dip continuity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine empirical data with scaled physical reasoning for geognosy
rubrics_metrics.description: It is by a combination of actual phenomena, by an ideal enlargement of relations in space, and of the amount of active forces, that we are able to advance into the long sought and indefinitely anticipated domain of geognosy, which has only within the last half century been based on the solid foundation of scientific deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synthesize field observations, measured quantities, and scaled reasoning about forces and time to produce geognostic models. Make explicit the scaling assumptions and force estimates used to extrapolate from observable to unobservable depths or times.
